newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - Brown to aim at Advance Corporation Tax.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Brown to aim at Advance Corporation Tax.

text.p: Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown's hit list for raising revenue in the July 2 budget will be topped by Advance Corporation Tax (ACT) and its accompanying tax break, a Reuters survey on Tuesday showed.

Companies pay ACT on their dividend payments to cover shareholders' tax liabilities and can then deduct the money from their corporation tax bill. Tax-exempt shareholders can then claim a refund on the dividend tax paid on their behalf.
Analysts estimate that full abolition of ACT would save the Treasury around five billion sterling per year whilst reducing it to 10 percent should garner nearly three billion sterling.

Of 20 economists Reuters asked between June 19 and 20 to predict the budget package, 17 expected some change to ACT. Six expected it to be reduced to 10 percent from the current level of 20 percent, and three expected it to be abolished altogether.
The rest were divided between predicting a rate of 15 percent, a phased reduction or a cut this time round but with no estimate of the level.

A 10 percent rate is particularly alluring given that it could be justified by delivering Labour's election pledge to introduce a new bottom rate of tax of 10 percent, half the current rate. Two of those expecting a new 10 percent ACT rate also expected a new 10 percent tax band.

Most of the analysts took the view that the recent spate of media reports suggesting some change to the ACT regime was on its way, meant that the Treasury was testing the waters through a series of leaks.
"I think some kind of move, probably down to 10 percent, is widely expected," said Andrew Schofield, senior economist at Business Strategies.

"They are quite limited on what they can do because of the manifesto commitments and ACT looks like a fairly painless option," he said. Using ACT as a revenue raiser is particularly attractive because it is unlikely to damage the ruling Labour Party's new-found credibility with voters -- it won the May 1 general election having endured 18 years in opposition.

Prime Minister Tony Blair will be determined not to be seen to renege on election promises not to increase taxation, so the corporate not the private sector will have to shoulder the burden of higher taxes.

The only squeals of dismay from a change to ACT are likely to come from tax-exempt bodies such as pension funds, horrified at losing the tax refund on dividend payments they receive under the current ACT system.

"Given that we already know they're going to cut VAT on fuel, without a reduction in ACT, we're looking at a net fiscal loosening," Co-operative Bank economist Andrew Snowball said. "ACT's going to be the main revenue raiser," he said.

Labour has pledged to reduce UK value added tax, a sales tax, on domestic fuel consumption to five percent from the level of eight percent imposed by the previous Conservative administration. This will cost around one billion sterling.
But the complexity of ACT may mean that pension funds could heave a sigh of relief at least until the November budget

"ACT is not something you can afford to rush. They've only been in power for a couple of months and they may not have had time to take a considered decision," said one economist surveyed, who did not want to be named.

"They've spent a lot of time trying to appear more business-friendly and waiting until November may make the whole thing seem less rushed," he said. He expected ACT to be abolished at the July budget. --London Polling Unit: +44 171 542 5109 email:
